questions.question: Define market failure precisely and explain its six causes, each with the mechanism that produces the wrong quantity.
questions.expected_answer: Market failure exists when markets allocate resources inefficiently — the quantity produced and consumed differs from the socially optimal quantity, so a different allocation could raise society's welfare; the definition concerns wrong quantities, not high prices or greedy firms. The six causes: (1) externalities — costs or benefits spill onto third parties outside the transaction, so the price ignores them and the quantity comes out wrong; (2) missing markets — public goods are non-rival and non-excludable, so no firm can charge users and the market never forms, while merit goods are under-consumed because people undervalue or cannot afford them and demerit goods are over-consumed; (3) imperfect competition — a monopolist holds price above marginal cost and output below the social optimum; (4) imperfect information — ignorant buyers, workers or lenders make wrong-quantity decisions; (5) immobility of factors — resources cannot move to their best use, as with retrenched workers whose skills fit no other industry, producing structural unemployment; (6) inequality — markets weigh demand by purchasing power, not need, so resources flow to luxuries while unmet essential needs carry no money votes. Efficiency and equity are separate tests.

questions.question: Using the brick kiln and the case of education, explain the externality diagrams and how the state's instruments push markets toward the social optimum.
questions.expected_answer: Private costs are the producer's own; external costs land on bystanders; social cost is their sum — and similarly for benefits. For a negative production externality (the smoky brick kiln): demand slopes down, the kiln's marginal private cost slopes up, and adding the external cost per unit gives a marginal social cost curve parallel above it. The market settles where demand crosses private cost — a large output at a low price; society's optimum is at the crossing with social cost — fewer units at a higher price. Goods with external costs are over-produced and under-priced. For a positive consumption externality (education and training): social benefit runs parallel above private demand, so the market quantity falls short of the social optimum — such goods are under-produced. Instruments: corrective taxes equal to the external cost (carbon tax, fuel levy, excise duties, the sugary drinks levy) lift private cost onto social cost so the market chooses the correct smaller quantity; subsidies on external benefits (no-fee schools, free clinics) lift private incentives to social ones; direct provision supplies public goods that markets never form; regulation sets direct rules where prices are too blunt; maximum and minimum prices protect consumers or suppliers at the risk of shortages or surpluses; redistribution answers inequality. Each instrument carries its own cost — wrong tax levels, financing burdens, public-sector weaknesses — so each intervention must justify itself case by case.

questions.question: Describe the five steps of cost-benefit analysis, explain why it is the right tool for public projects like the toll road, and state its four main limits.
questions.expected_answer: Steps: (1) identify every cost — construction and operation, plus displaced households, lost farmland, bypassed traders, noise; (2) identify every benefit — output, time saved, accidents avoided, jobs, wider economic gains; (3) attach money values even to unpriced items — time at the wage rate, a wetland at the cost of equivalent treatment, risk to life via measured willingness to pay; (4) discount future flows, because a rand years away is worth less than a rand today; (5) compare — proceed if social benefits exceed social costs, and rank rival projects by benefit-cost ratio when budgets are scarce. CBA suits public projects because it writes into the ledger exactly what markets omit: externalities, unpriced goods and third parties — it asks what the road does to everyone, not what it earns at the boom. Limits: valuing the unpriceable is contested; the discount rate is a moral choice disguised as arithmetic — a high rate silences future generations; project champions overstate benefits and understate costs (optimism bias); and CBA sums rands without asking whose, so a passing project can still load its costs onto the poorest — distribution and compensation of losers must be judged alongside the total.
